WESTERN SAHARA / SEPARATE TERRITORY
Western Sahara
A disputed territory, with different claims and different areas of control.
WHY IT HAS ITS OWN SECTION
Western Sahara is listed by the United Nations as a Non-Self-Governing Territory.
Morocco claims and administers most of it. The Polisario Front seeks independence
through the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, recognised by some states and a member
of the African Union. Neither a Moroccan administrative map nor the Sahrawi claim alone
explains the whole situation.
LAND, CITIES AND NEIGHBOURS
The Atlantic lies to the west; Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania are the land neighbours.
Laayoune and Dakhla are major cities. The interior is dry, with pastoral traditions and
phosphate deposits. A defensive berm separates most Moroccan-administered territory
from areas to its east. Sahrawi refugee camps near Tindouf are in Algeria, not in Western
Sahara.

Morocco

sovereignty.

How this edition was made
MAPS
World and regional coasts use an open geographic dataset, with the official Indian outline

landforms use named point locations, not a shaded-elevation model. Distant islands have

[1] AFRICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own

WHAT IS INCLUDED
All 54 widely recognised sovereign countries in Africa receive complete chapters. Western
Sahara has a separate section because its sovereignty is disputed. The African Union’s
membership count differs: it includes the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Other
territories and disputed places appear in the closing notes.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Uganda and Botswana use broad geographic regions; Libya uses a clearly dated
historical district framework. These are not complete directories of current local councils.

dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the tables;
where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older internal
borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current affairs

repeats it at a larger scale. Other disputed borders and territorial claims are explained
where relevant; map colour alone should not be read as a legal ruling.

[1] ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES

[2] APPENDIX B / BORDERS AND ADMINISTRATION
When a line needs an explanation
KASHMIR AND THE INDIA–CHINA FRONTIER
India, Pakistan and China claim or administer different parts of the wider Kashmir region.
India’s official outline includes territory outside its actual control, including areas
administered by Pakistan and China. The claimed Indian border with Afghanistan depends
on this convention. Pakistan’s directory separately describes areas it administers. Border
notes distinguish claims, control and the map convention rather than silently substituting
one for another.
TAIWAN, HONG KONG AND MACAO
Taiwan has its own government and institutions and is claimed by the People’s Republic of
China. Its international recognition is limited and disputed. Hong Kong and Macao are
special administrative regions of the People’s Republic, with separate legal and currency
arrangements. They are included within the China chapter and directory, not counted as
independent countries.
THE KOREAN PENINSULA
North and South Korea are separate states. The Korean War ended with an armistice in
1953, not a peace treaty. The Demilitarized Zone and related military lines are not

MALDIVES / HISTORY
How the present took shape
EARLIER LIVES AND TURNING POINTS
The islands had maritime connections with South Asia and Arabia. Islam became
established in the twelfth century. A long sultanate history was followed by British
protection from 1887. Independence came in 1965, and a republic was established in
1968. Multiparty politics developed through later constitutional changes.
GOVERNMENT, WORK AND PUBLIC LIFE
Tourism and fishing support the economy. Resorts and inhabited islands can have very
different services and daily routines. Imported food, fuel and construction materials make
shipping costs important. Political competition has produced changes of government.
Local administration changed again in 2026, when atoll councils were abolished; the
geographic atoll directory is therefore labelled as a reference framework.

APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES AND SPECIAL PLACES
Places between the country chapters
Gibraltar and the British bases in Cyprus
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with a land border with Spain. Akrotiri and Dhekelia
are British Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus. They are distinct from the United Kingdom
itself and from the Republic of Cyprus.
Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
These are Crown Dependencies, not part of the United Kingdom. Jersey and Guernsey lie
near France; the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea. They govern many of their own domestic
affairs.
Faroe Islands and Greenland
Both are self-governing parts of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Faroes lie in the North
Atlantic. Greenland is geographically in North America and shares a land boundary with
Canada on Hans Island.
Åland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen
Åland is an autonomous region of Finland, with Swedish as its official language. Svalbard is
Norwegian territory governed under a special treaty framework. Jan Mayen is also
Norwegian territory, with no permanent civilian community.
References: UK Foreign Office · Government of Norway · Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Status reference date:
11 October 2026.

WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA B.4

[2] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[3] NORTH AMERICA / REGIONAL OVERVIEW
The Caribbean’s 13 sovereign states
Some countries occupy one main island. Others include part of a larger
island or a chain of smaller ones.
Cuba
Haiti Dominican
Republic Jamaica
Bahamas
Barbados
Antigua and
Barbuda
Saint Kitts
and Nevis Dominica
Saint Lucia
Saint Vincent and
the Grenadines
Grenada
Trinidad and
Tobago
Shared waters, different states
Haiti and the Dominican Republic share Hispaniola. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and
Grenada divide the Grenadine island chain between them. The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic,
north of the main Antillean arc.
Countries and other places
Puerto Rico, Martinique, Guadeloupe and several other islands are not sovereign states. Their
separate constitutional arrangements appear in Appendix B. The overview highlights the 13
sovereign states in green.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA F.3

[4] APPENDIX B / NON-SOVEREIGN PLACES
North America beyond its sovereign states
These places belong in a geographic portrait of the region. Their legal
arrangements differ, so they are not counted among the 23 sovereign
countries.

thousands of years.

it. A family in Toronto, a fishing crew in Newfoundland and an Inuit household in Nunavut share a
country, but their daily lives can be very different. Canada’s story is about those differences as

[4] CANADA / SOCIETY
Living in Canada
A winter coat belongs in the picture. So do rent payments, long
commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.

Across the country
The west coast is not the same as the Prairies. Quebec is not the
same as Atlantic Canada. A few stops reveal how much changes
along the way.
Vancouver: a Pacific port city beside mountains and
coastal waters.
Lake Louise and Mirror Lake in the Canadian Rockies.
British Columbia
Vancouver connects Canada with Pacific trade.
Coastal forests, mountains and fishing
communities share the province with drier
inland valleys. Vancouver Island contains
Victoria, the provincial capital. Indigenous
nations have long histories throughout these
lands.
The Prairies
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba contain
farmland, cities and major resource industries.
Winnipeg has deep Métis connections. Calgary
and Edmonton grew with western
development. Prairie life includes cold winters,
big skies and sharp arguments about energy
and federal policy.
Ontario
Toronto is a centre of finance and migration.
Ottawa holds federal institutions. Outside the
southern urban corridor are smaller towns,
forests and mining communities. Northern
Ontario has its own concerns about distance,
services and land.
Quebec
French language, civil law and a strong sense
of national identity shape the province.
Montreal is its largest city; Quebec City is its
capital. The St. Lawrence has long carried
trade and settlement. The province also
includes far northern communities with
different histories.
Atlantic Canada
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward
Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador look
towards the Atlantic. Fishing, ports and
migration connect them with the wider world.
Acadian communities have a distinct
French-speaking heritage. Labrador and the
island of Newfoundland differ greatly in
landscape and culture.
The three territories

[6] CANADA / GEOGRAPHY
A country on three oceans
Canada faces the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans. With about
9.98 million square kilometres of land and inland water, it is the
world’s second-largest country by total area.

Selected cities and neighbouring lands. Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The land neighbours
The United States borders Canada to the
south and through Alaska in the northwest. A
2022 agreement with the Kingdom of
Denmark, together with Greenland, divided
Tartupaluk/Hans Island and established
another land boundary.
Mountains, plains and rivers
The Rockies rise in the west. Mount Logan, in
Yukon’s Saint Elias Mountains, is Canada’s
highest peak. Farther east lie the Prairies and
the old rock of the Canadian Shield. The
Mackenzie river system drains towards the
Arctic; the St. Lawrence connects the Great
Lakes with the Atlantic.
Islands and fresh water
Baffin Island, in Nunavut, is Canada’s
largest island. Newfoundland and Vancouver
Island are other major islands. Lakes cover
large areas of the country. Four of the five
Great Lakes lie on the Canada-US border; Lake
Michigan is wholly in the United States.
Not one climate
Coastal British Columbia has relatively mild
winters. The Prairies face bigger seasonal
extremes. Arctic communities have long,
severe winters, while southern cities can have
hot summers. Canada is cold, but not cold in
the same way everywhere.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.5

[7] CANADA / CULTURE AND SCIENCE
Stories, music and discovery
Canadian culture comes from many languages and communities.
Some of its best-known works ask who belongs, whose history is
remembered and what the landscape means.
Books and stories
Margaret Atwood writes about power and
social control. Alice Munro found complex lives
in apparently ordinary places. Michael
Ondaatje explores memory and displacement.
Quebec’s literature has a rich French-language
tradition. Indigenous writers, including Thomas
King and Lee Maracle, challenge inherited
accounts of the country.
Music and performance
Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell and Céline Dion
reached listeners around the world. Inuit throat
singing and First Nations musical traditions
belong to distinct communities, not a single
generic style. Contemporary Indigenous artists
combine older practices with new forms on
their own terms.
Art and film
The Group of Seven helped make landscape
painting part of national identity. Inuit
sculpture and printmaking offer other ways of
seeing land and life. Canadian filmmaking
includes English, French and Indigenous work,
while cities such as Toronto and Vancouver
also host international productions.
Sport and public ritual
Ice hockey is the national winter sport;
lacrosse is the national summer sport. Both are
named in federal law. Lacrosse has Indigenous
origins. Fans also follow basketball, football
and other games. Local rinks and school teams
matter as much to everyday sport as
professional stars.
Science that changed lives
Research in Toronto led to insulin’s first
successful clinical use in 1922. Frederick
Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and John
Macleod all played roles. The treatment
changed diabetes care. Canada’s scientific
history also includes space robotics, medical

[8] CANADA / THE FEDERATION
Ten provinces, three territories
Each has its own government and capital. Their names matter: much
of Canadian politics turns on what should be decided locally and
what should be decided in Ottawa.

Manitoba Winnipeg 1870
Ontario Toronto 1867
Quebec Quebec City 1867

Northwest Territories once covered a much larger area.
WHY “PROVINCE” AND “TERRITORY” ARE DIFFERENT
Provincial powers are set out in the Constitution. Territorial powers are largely delegated by
federal law, though elected territorial governments now exercise substantial authority.
Indigenous governments add another important layer.

sources.text:
CANADA / SOCIETY
Living in Canada
A winter coat belongs in the picture. So do rent payments, long
commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.

[4] CANADA / POLITICS
How Canada is governed
Canadians elect members of Parliament. The government must keep
the confidence of the House of Commons to remain in office.
Parliament Hill, Ottawa: the centre of federal political life.
The Crown and the government
Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The
sovereign is head of state, represented
federally by the governor general. The prime
minister leads the government. These roles
differ: the head of state is not the elected head
of government.
Parliament and elections
Parliament consists of the Crown, the elected
House of Commons and the appointed Senate.
Voters choose a local MP, rather than voting
directly for prime minister. The person able to
command Commons confidence forms a
government. A party can govern with a
majority or seek support from others.
A federal country
Ottawa handles national matters such as
defence and foreign affairs. Provinces have
major responsibilities for education, healthcare
and civil law. Territories have their own elected
governments. Indigenous governments
exercise powers through different legal and
political arrangements.
Rights and legal traditions
The Charter protects rights and freedoms,
subject to constitutional rules and limits.
Courts interpret those rules. Quebec uses civil
law for most private-law matters, while other
provinces mainly use common law. Federal law
and Indigenous legal traditions add further
layers.

[5] CANADA / HISTORY / COLONIES
French and British North America
European newcomers depended on Indigenous knowledge and
partnerships. Over time, trade and settlement gave way to larger

Old Quebec. French language and architecture remain central to the city.
Across the Atlantic
Norse visitors reached what is now

New France

[2] USA / INTRODUCTION
Getting to know the USA
A New York subway ride and a drive across rural Montana belong to
the same country. They can feel like different worlds.
The United States began as thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast. Its borders later reached
the Pacific, Alaska and Hawaii. That expansion brought opportunity for some and dispossession for
others. The country’s history includes invention and migration, slavery and freedom, and repeated
arguments over who has a voice.

THREE PLACES OFTEN CONFUSED
Washington, D.C. is the national capital. Washington state is on the Pacific coast. New York
City is the country’s largest city, but Albany is New York state’s capital.

Stars and stripes
The fifty stars represent the fifty states. The
thirteen stripes recall the original colonies. The
present fifty-star design has been used since
1960, after Hawaii became a state.

CHAPTER 2 / UNITED STATES 2.7

[4] USA / BEYOND THE STATES
Washington and the territories
The United States is more than fifty states. A federal district and
island territories have different political arrangements.
Washington, D.C.
The capital sits beside the Potomac River. It is
a federal district, not part of any state.
Residents elect local officials and take part in
presidential elections, but the district has no
voting senators or voting representative in the
House. Congress has special authority over it.
The five inhabited territories
Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands lie in
the Caribbean. Guam, the Northern Mariana
Islands and American Samoa lie in the
Pacific. Each has a local government. Their
constitutional position differs from that of
states.
Citizenship and representation
People born in most of these territories are US
citizens. People born in American Samoa are
generally US nationals at birth rather than
citizens, unless another rule applies. Territorial
residents do not vote for president in the
general election while residing there. Their
congressional delegates or resident
commissioner cannot vote on final House
passage.
Island names worth knowing
Puerto Rico is both a territory and its main
island; Vieques and Culebra belong to it. The
US Virgin Islands include St. Croix, St.
Thomas and St. John. The Northern Mariana
Islands include Saipan, Tinian and Rota.
Tutuila is the main population centre of
American Samoa; Guam is an island in its own
right.
Other US island possessions
The US Minor Outlying Islands include Baker,
Howland, Jarvis and Navassa islands; Johnston,
Midway and Palmyra atolls; Kingman Reef; and
Wake Island. Most have no permanent civilian
population. Some sovereignty claims are
disputed, including Navassa with Haiti and
Wake with the Marshall Islands.

[5] USA / GOVERNMENT
How the republic works
Americans elect a president separately from Congress. Power is
divided between federal institutions, states and local governments.
The US Capitol in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets.
Congress makes federal laws
The House of Representatives has 435 voting
seats, apportioned among states by
population. The Senate has two members from
each state, making 100 senators. House
members serve two-year terms; senators serve
six. Both chambers must agree on legislation
before it reaches the president.
The president and the courts
The president heads the executive branch and
serves a four-year term, subject to
constitutional limits. The Supreme Court and
lower federal courts interpret laws and hear
cases. Federal judges are nominated by the
president and confirmed by the Senate.
Different branches can check one another’s
powers.
The Electoral College
Presidential elections are decided through
electoral votes, not simply the nationwide
popular vote. States and D.C. appoint electors.
Most states award all their electoral votes to
the statewide winner; Maine and Nebraska use
different rules. This system makes the
geography of votes especially important.
States, rights and disagreement
States govern many matters involving schools,
policing, roads and elections, within federal law
and the Constitution. Tribal governments have
a distinct position. Constitutional rights are
interpreted through courts and political
disputes. Democratic and Republican parties
dominate national elections, but each contains
different views.

The United Kingdom contains England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. They share a

USA / BEYOND THE STATES
Washington and the territories
The United States is more than fifty states. A federal district and
island territories have different political arrangements.
Washington, D.C.
The capital sits beside the Potomac River. It is
a federal district, not part of any state.
Residents elect local officials and take part in
presidential elections, but the district has no
voting senators or voting representative in the
House. Congress has special authority over it.
The five inhabited territories
Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands lie in
the Caribbean. Guam, the Northern Mariana
Islands and American Samoa lie in the
Pacific. Each has a local government. Their
constitutional position differs from that of
states.
Citizenship and representation
People born in most of these territories are US
citizens. People born in American Samoa are
generally US nationals at birth rather than
citizens, unless another rule applies. Territorial
residents do not vote for president in the
general election while residing there. Their
congressional delegates or resident
commissioner cannot vote on final House
passage.
Island names worth knowing
Puerto Rico is both a territory and its main
island; Vieques and Culebra belong to it. The
US Virgin Islands include St. Croix, St.
Thomas and St. John. The Northern Mariana
Islands include Saipan, Tinian and Rota.
Tutuila is the main population centre of
American Samoa; Guam is an island in its own
right.
Other US island possessions
The US Minor Outlying Islands include Baker,
Howland, Jarvis and Navassa islands; Johnston,
Midway and Palmyra atolls; Kingman Reef; and
Wake Island. Most have no permanent civilian
population. Some sovereignty claims are
disputed, including Navassa with Haiti and
Wake with the Marshall Islands.

sources.name: North_America.pdf
sources.text:
USA / GOVERNMENT
How the republic works
Americans elect a president separately from Congress. Power is
divided between federal institutions, states and local governments.
The US Capitol in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets.
Congress makes federal laws
The House of Representatives has 435 voting
seats, apportioned among states by
population. The Senate has two members from
each state, making 100 senators. House
members serve two-year terms; senators serve
six. Both chambers must agree on legislation
before it reaches the president.
The president and the courts
The president heads the executive branch and
serves a four-year term, subject to
constitutional limits. The Supreme Court and
lower federal courts interpret laws and hear
cases. Federal judges are nominated by the
president and confirmed by the Senate.
Different branches can check one another’s
powers.
The Electoral College
Presidential elections are decided through
electoral votes, not simply the nationwide
popular vote. States and D.C. appoint electors.
Most states award all their electoral votes to
the statewide winner; Maine and Nebraska use
different rules. This system makes the
geography of votes especially important.
States, rights and disagreement
States govern many matters involving schools,
policing, roads and elections, within federal law
and the Constitution. Tribal governments have
a distinct position. Constitutional rights are
interpreted through courts and political
disputes. Democratic and Republican parties
dominate national elections, but each contains
different views.
CHAPTER 2 / UNITED STATES 2.14

Saint Martin and Sint Maarten share an island. The northern part is a French overseas

This volume follows the broad North American scope of the UN M49 grouping: Northern

The Caribbean’s 13 sovereign states
Some countries occupy one main island. Others include part of a larger
island or a chain of smaller ones.
Cuba

Bahamas

Shared waters, different states
Haiti and the Dominican Republic share Hispaniola. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and
Grenada divide the Grenadine island chain between them. The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic,
north of the main Antillean arc.
Countries and other places
Puerto Rico, Martinique, Guadeloupe and several other islands are not sovereign states. Their
separate constitutional arrangements appear in Appendix B. The overview highlights the 13
sovereign states in green.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA F.3

[3] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[4] MEXICO / THE WIDER WORLD
Mexico beyond its borders
Mexico belongs to North America geographically and has deep
connections across Latin America and the wider world.
The United States and Canada

United States and New Zealand
GUAM
U.S. territory; main government centre Hagåtña. The island is home to Chamorro heritage

NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS
A commonwealth in political union with the United States; Saipan is the main government
centre. The islands include Saipan, Tinian, Rota and northern volcanic islands.
AMERICAN SAMOA
U.S. territory centred on Tutuila and the Pago Pago harbour area, with government
institutions at Fagatogo and Utulei. The Manuʻa group and other islands broaden the map.

TOKELAU
New Zealand territory consisting of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo. Decisions involve
island institutions and a national General Fono. There is no single conventional capital
city.
HAWAIʻI
A U.S. state, not a dependent territory or separate country. Honolulu is the capital.
Hawaiian language and culture, the overthrow of the kingdom and annexation belong
within its history.
U.S. MINOR OUTLYING ISLANDS
Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Johnston, Kingman Reef, Midway, Palmyra and Wake have
different administrative and environmental roles. They are not added as independent
countries.

[8] NAURU / HISTORY
How the present took shape
EARLIER LIVES AND TURNING POINTS
Nauruan communities lived on the island before German annexation in 1888. Phosphate
discovery brought intensive extraction and foreign control. Australia, New Zealand and
Britain administered the island after the First World War. Japanese occupation during the
Second World War included deportation and suffering. Independence came in 1968.
GOVERNMENT, WORK AND PUBLIC LIFE
Parliament elects a president who serves as both head of state and head of government.
Fourteen districts are listed, but they do not have fourteen separate provincial capitals.
Phosphate income once supported considerable wealth; depletion and financial problems
changed that position. Fishing revenues, services and arrangements connected with
Australia have shaped recent finances. Offshore migration processing has also drawn
major human-rights scrutiny.
This 2007 photograph records phosphate mining and its effects on the land. Resource extraction brought
income but also left a lasting environmental burden.

A region connected by ocean
THE COUNTRIES

New Zealand lead, followed by the independent Pacific island states. The Cook Islands and

dependent territories; a separate section explains them. Other territories and Pacific
places are identified with their constitutional links.

Every country has three different images: its opener, a history illustration and a culture or
daily-life image. Historic documents and photographs are identified in captions. Images
are not generated scenes. Photographer and licence credits link to the original records.
The pictures are not reused between chapters.

Population uses UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand, except Samoa’s
official November 2021 census. These dates are printed beside the figures. Directories
state their level: provinces, states, districts, councils or, for Kiribati, statistical districts. A
reference centre is not automatically a separate capital.

The Pacific-centred views carry longitudes eastward beyond 180 degrees. This joins
islands that ordinary world maps split at the edge. It does not change their locations or
political status. Small islands have point markers and insets; dots are deliberately larger
than the land so the reader can find them. Insets have different scales. Sea neighbours are
selected nearby countries, not claims about maritime borders.
PAGE NUMBERS AND MAP CONVENTIONS
Country pages use 1.1, 1.2 and so on. PDF bookmarks open complete chapters; there is no
printed index.

[3] OCEANIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A region connected by ocean
THE COUNTRIES
This volume has fourteen chapters for Oceania’s UN-member countries. Australia and
New Zealand lead, followed by the independent Pacific island states. The Cook Islands and
Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand, not ordinary
dependent territories; a separate section explains them. Other territories and Pacific
places are identified with their constitutional links.
PICTURES THAT BELONG TO THE STORY
Every country has three different images: its opener, a history illustration and a culture or
daily-life image. Historic documents and photographs are identified in captions. Images
are not generated scenes. Photographer and licence credits link to the original records.
The pictures are not reused between chapters.
DATES AND ADMINISTRATIVE LEVELS
Population uses UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand, except Samoa’s
official November 2021 census. These dates are printed beside the figures. Directories
state their level: provinces, states, districts, councils or, for Kiribati, statistical districts. A
reference centre is not automatically a separate capital.
READING AN ISLAND MAP
The Pacific-centred views carry longitudes eastward beyond 180 degrees. This joins
islands that ordinary world maps split at the edge. It does not change their locations or
political status. Small islands have point markers and insets; dots are deliberately larger
than the land so the reader can find them. Insets have different scales. Sea neighbours are
selected nearby countries, not claims about maritime borders.
PAGE NUMBERS AND MAP CONVENTIONS
Country pages use 1.1, 1.2 and so on. PDF bookmarks open complete chapters; there is no
printed index.

[4] PACIFIC TERRITORIES / DIRECTORY

RAPA NUI / EASTER ISLAND
Part of Chile, geographically and culturally connected to Polynesia. Hanga Roa is the main
settlement. Moai, land, heritage and local rights belong in a story larger than a
remote-island photograph.
WESTERN NEW GUINEA
The western part of New Guinea is administered by Indonesia, whose country chapter
belongs in the Asia volume. Indigenous identities and political conflict should not
disappear because of a statistical continental grouping.
BOUGAINVILLE
An autonomous region within Papua New Guinea. The 2019 referendum and continuing
constitutional process are explained in that chapter; the island is not counted as an
already independent country.
ANTARCTIC CLAIMS
Claims linked to Australia, New Zealand and other states fall under the Antarctic Treaty
system. This volume does not add Antarctic territory to Oceania’s list of independent
countries.
REGIONAL ORGANISATIONS
The Pacific Islands Forum includes countries and some territories. The Pacific Community
supports technical and development cooperation. Membership in a regional organisation
does not make every participant’s legal status identical.

A region connected by ocean

This volume has fourteen chapters for Oceania’s UN-member countries. Australia and
New Zealand lead, followed by the independent Pacific island states. The Cook Islands and

dependent territories; a separate section explains them. Other territories and Pacific
places are identified with their constitutional links.

daily-life image. Historic documents and photographs are identified in captions. Images
are not generated scenes. Photographer and licence credits link to the original records.

Population uses UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand, except Samoa’s
official November 2021 census. These dates are printed beside the figures. Directories
state their level: provinces, states, districts, councils or, for Kiribati, statistical districts. A
reference centre is not automatically a separate capital.

islands that ordinary world maps split at the edge. It does not change their locations or
political status. Small islands have point markers and insets; dots are deliberately larger
than the land so the reader can find them. Insets have different scales. Sea neighbours are
selected nearby countries, not claims about maritime borders.

[1] ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own

WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This

World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate

explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026

WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA B.2

[3] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[7] APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES
Places that need an extra note
RÉUNION AND MAYOTTE
Réunion and Mayotte are French overseas departments in the Indian Ocean. Mayotte
belongs geographically to the Comoros archipelago; Comoros claims it, while France
administers it. Neither is one of the 54 sovereign country chapters.
CEUTA, MELILLA AND THE CANARY ISLANDS
Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish autonomous cities on the North African coast, claimed by
Morocco. Spain’s Canary Islands lie in the Atlantic off northwest Africa. They have no
separate sovereign-country chapter.
SAINT HELENA, ASCENSION AND TRISTAN DA CUNHA
These widely separated Atlantic islands form one British Overseas Territory. Separate
insets are necessary to show their distances. Their connection to Africa is geographic, not
membership among African sovereign states.
CHAGOS AND TROMELIN
Mauritius claims the Chagos Archipelago and Tromelin. The UK and Mauritius signed a
Chagos agreement in 2025, with implementation contested in 2026. France administers
Tromelin. Maps should distinguish claims, treaties and completed transfers.
SOMALILAND
Somaliland has separate institutions and declared independence in 1991. Israel
recognised it in December 2025; Somalia and the African Union reject its separation. The
Somalia chapter uses the prevailing international country outline and explains the limited
recognition.
ABYEI AND OTHER CONTESTED BOUNDARIES
Abyei’s final status remains disputed between Sudan and South Sudan. The Egypt–Sudan
boundary dispute includes Halaib; Kenya–South Sudan claims overlap in the Ilemi
Triangle. Lake Malawi/Nyasa has a Tanzania–Malawi boundary dispute. Regional locators
do not replace legal or diplomatic boundary documentation.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / AFRICA B.1

[8] AFRICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
All 54 widely recognised sovereign countries in Africa receive complete chapters. Western
Sahara has a separate section because its sovereignty is disputed. The African Union’s
membership count differs: it includes the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Other
territories and disputed places appear in the closing notes.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Uganda and Botswana use broad geographic regions; Libya uses a clearly dated
historical district framework. These are not complete directories of current local councils.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. They are
dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the tables;
where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older internal
borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current affairs
were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES
Every world locator uses the official Survey of India international outline. The appendix
repeats it at a larger scale. Other disputed borders and territorial claims are explained
where relevant; map colour alone should not be read as a legal ruling.
FINDING YOUR WAY

chapters and major sections.

NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES
Places that need an extra note
RÉUNION AND MAYOTTE
Réunion and Mayotte are French overseas departments in the Indian Ocean. Mayotte
belongs geographically to the Comoros archipelago; Comoros claims it, while France
administers it. Neither is one of the 54 sovereign country chapters.
CEUTA, MELILLA AND THE CANARY ISLANDS
Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish autonomous cities on the North African coast, claimed by
Morocco. Spain’s Canary Islands lie in the Atlantic off northwest Africa. They have no
separate sovereign-country chapter.
SAINT HELENA, ASCENSION AND TRISTAN DA CUNHA
These widely separated Atlantic islands form one British Overseas Territory. Separate
insets are necessary to show their distances. Their connection to Africa is geographic, not
membership among African sovereign states.
CHAGOS AND TROMELIN
Mauritius claims the Chagos Archipelago and Tromelin. The UK and Mauritius signed a
Chagos agreement in 2025, with implementation contested in 2026. France administers
Tromelin. Maps should distinguish claims, treaties and completed transfers.
SOMALILAND
Somaliland has separate institutions and declared independence in 1991. Israel
recognised it in December 2025; Somalia and the African Union reject its separation. The
Somalia chapter uses the prevailing international country outline and explains the limited
recognition.
ABYEI AND OTHER CONTESTED BOUNDARIES
Abyei’s final status remains disputed between Sudan and South Sudan. The Egypt–Sudan
boundary dispute includes Halaib; Kenya–South Sudan claims overlap in the Ilemi
Triangle. Lake Malawi/Nyasa has a Tanzania–Malawi boundary dispute. Regional locators
do not replace legal or diplomatic boundary documentation.

AFRICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
All 54 widely recognised sovereign countries in Africa receive complete chapters. Western
Sahara has a separate section because its sovereignty is disputed. The African Union’s
membership count differs: it includes the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Other
territories and disputed places appear in the closing notes.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Uganda and Botswana use broad geographic regions; Libya uses a clearly dated
historical district framework. These are not complete directories of current local councils.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. They are
dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the tables;
where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older internal
borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current affairs
were checked for this October 2026 edition.

repeats it at a larger scale. Other disputed borders and territorial claims are explained
where relevant; map colour alone should not be read as a legal ruling.

[1] # FreeEdit — Product Improvements & Engineering Roadmap

> **Goal:** Turn FreeEdit into a dependable, frictionless way to clean up a recording and export a shareable result — without becoming a bloated video editor.

**Repository:** https://github.com/srbmaury/FreeEdit 
**Document type:** Product and technical improvement proposal 
**Guiding principle:** **Upload → make a few useful edits → preview → export.**

---

## 1. Product Direction

FreeEdit already targets a clear user problem: quick audio/video cleanup. The existing project, as previously reviewed, includes noise reduction using DeepFilterNet3, video trimming, text overlays, blurring/pixelation, previews, and export via a FastAPI/FFmpeg-based processing pipeline.

**Keep the product focused:** A user with a noisy screen recording should be able to make it watchable and shareable in one session. Avoid accounts, social features, collaboration systems, and general-purpose timeline editing in the first release.

### Primary user journey

1. **Drop** a recorded video or audio file into FreeEdit.
2. **Choose** a quick cleanup action (noise removal, trim, silence cleanup, or privacy masking).
3. **Review** a fast preview and adjust the results if needed.
4. **Export** the finished media with an appropriate size/quality preset.
5. **Leave** with the processed file; account creation should not be required.

**North-star metric:** Percentage of successful uploads that produce an exported file. 
**Secondary metrics:** Median time-to-export; processing failure rate; failed export rate; repeat-use rate (if measured in a privacy-preserving way).

---

## 2. Features to Add (Prioritized)

### P0 — One-click silence removal

**Problem:** Tutorial, lecture, and screen recordings commonly contain awkward pauses.

[2] ependency compliance.

### Phase 2 — Strongest new editing feature

- [ ] Detect silent intervals.
- [ ] Let users preview and toggle proposed cuts.
- [ ] Export synchronized concatenated media.
- [ ] Test edge cases and browser playback.

### Phase 3 — Make sharing easier

- [ ] Build opaque privacy masks with time ranges.
- [ ] Add guided output presets.
- [ ] Show a pre-export summary of changes and expected output.

### Explicitly out of scope

- Multi-track professional editing timeline.
- AI-generated content or AI chat interface.
- Cloud project collaboration.
- Public content feeds or social sharing network.
- Mandatory sign-in for basic edits.

---

## 6. Definition of Success

A first-time user can upload a typical screen recording, remove background noise, shorten pauses, hide one on-screen detail, preview the result, and export a playable file **without help or an account**.

> **FreeEdit should feel like a utility, not a video-production platform.**

[3] # Seven Practical Open-Source Project Ideas

> **Theme:** One recognizable problem. One complete user journey. One useful output. 
> **Constraints:** No forced sign-up, no AI wrapper, no social graph, no marketplace needed to deliver first-session value.

These are product concepts, **not claims that no competing products exist**. Each idea should be validated against available tools and with a handful of actual users before building extensively.

---

## Quick Comparison

| # | Project | User's job-to-be-done | Difficulty | Strongest differentiator to explore |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | GhostLayer | Remove unintended information from files | Medium | Inspect → explain → clean → verify |
| 02 | DiffPaper | Understand what changed between two PDFs | High | Layout-aware comparison and readable report |
| 03 | TableLift | Export messy webpage tables cleanly | Medium | Visual selection and reliable normalization |
| 04 | ProofPack | Capture an actionable bug report | High | Replay context with privacy controls |
| 05 | NearDrop | Transfer files directly between devices | High | Smooth cross-platform pairing/resume |
| 06 | SubShift | Fix subtitle timing | Low–Medium | Simple visual drift correction |
| 07 | FormForge | Fill non-interactive PDFs | Medium | Precise WYSIWYG placement and export |

---

## 01 — GhostLayer

**Tagline:** Know what a file reveals before you share it.

### Problem

Images can contain camera/GPS metadata. Documents can contain authorship, comments, tracked revisions, attachments, or other nonobvious information. Users rarely inspect these before sharing.

### Single user journey

`Drop file → Inspect metadata/hidden content → Select safe removals → Verify preview → Download cleaned copy`

### MVP

[4] e possible (idempotent submission or job reuse).

---

## 4. Suggested Architecture

**Keep it simple until there is real load.** A single service can remain the starting point.

```text
Browser (upload + edit instructions + preview)
 │
 ▼
FastAPI API ──> Job admission/validation ──> Bounded processing queue
 │ │
 │ ▼
 ├──> Status and error reporting FFmpeg + noise model
 │ │
 └──> Signed/authorized download <── Final output + retention cleanup
```

**Potential upgrades, not mandatory for MVP:** SQLite/PostgreSQL for durable job metadata, Redis/worker queue for multi-instance deployment, object storage if the platform's filesystem is ephemeral, and WebSockets or server-sent events if polling becomes awkward.

### Data model sketch

```text
MediaJob {
 id, status, input_metadata, edit_instructions,
 output_preset, progress, created_at, expires_at,
 error_code, output_location
}
```

For editing instructions, use versioned typed objects: `Trim`, `NoiseReduction`, `SilenceRemoval`, `Mask`, `TextOverlay`. This makes the frontend and worker agree on what is permitted.

---

## 5. Build Order

### Phase 1 — Make existing FreeEdit dependable

- [ ] Verify the current production flow end to end.
- [ ] Add job-aware cleanup and limits for CPU, memory, disk, and duration.
- [ ] Validate edit requests with typed models.
- [ ] Add baseline media regression tests (audio-only, video-only, VFR, portrait, corrupt input, large upload).
- [ ] Report clear processing errors and recovery actions.
- [ ] Review license and dependency compliance.

### Phase 2 — Strongest new editing feature

- [ ] Detect silent intervals.
- [ ] Let users preview and toggle proposed cuts.
- [ ] Export synchronized concatenated media.
- [ ] Test edge cases and browser playback.

[5] ed or constrained. Respect website access controls and terms. 
**Why useful:** Makes recurring data collection much less error-prone.

---

## 04 — ProofPack

**Tagline:** A bug report that engineers can actually investigate.

### Problem

A screenshot of an error often lacks steps to reproduce, console messages, and relevant browser/network context.

### Single user journey

`Start capture → Reproduce problem → Stop → Review/redact data → Export shareable report`

### MVP

- [ ] Opt-in tab recording or screenshots.
- [ ] Capture page URL, browser version, console errors, and failed network request metadata where allowed.
- [ ] Let the user annotate reproduction steps.
- [ ] Review and redact captured sensitive information.
- [ ] Export a ZIP with media, timeline, and standalone HTML summary.

### Version 2

- Time-correlated error timeline.
- Reusable issue templates.
- Optional integrations with issue trackers.

**Suggested stack:** TypeScript + browser extension APIs + IndexedDB. 
**Hardest problem:** Recording enough debugging context without capturing passwords, tokens, request bodies, or personal content. Collect a minimal safe default dataset and require explicit opt-in for anything more sensitive. 
**Why useful:** Converts a vague bug complaint into reproducible evidence.

---

## 05 — NearDrop

**Tagline:** Share a file directly with a nearby device, regardless of OS.

### Problem

Cross-platform file transfer can be cumbersome, especially across phones and computers using different ecosystems.

### Single user journey

`Choose file → Scan receiver's pairing QR → Receiver approves → Transfer → Verify checksum`

### MVP

- [ ] Discover or pair devices on the same local network.
- [ ] Establish an authenticated encrypted transfer session.

[6] demand**, not on a novelty score.

1. **Easiest first-use demonstration:** SubShift, FormForge, GhostLayer.
2. **Strongest technical depth:** DiffPaper, ProofPack, NearDrop.
3. **Best fit for a browser extension:** TableLift, ProofPack.
4. **Best local-first privacy angle:** GhostLayer, NearDrop, FormForge.

### Five-question validation checklist

- [ ] Can you describe the problem in one sentence without mentioning your technology?
- [ ] Can one user finish the full workflow alone?
- [ ] Is the result observable and genuinely useful?
- [ ] Have you tried the best existing alternatives and found a specific weakness?
- [ ] Can you build the smallest functional version without accounts or external dependencies?

### Suggested build discipline

```text
Week 1: Validate user journey and prototype the hardest technical step.
Week 2: Make a complete input → processing → output path.
Week 3: Test real files and failure modes.
Week 4: Polish, publish, collect feedback, and cut unused features.
```

*This is an illustrative schedule, not a promise that every project can be completed in four weeks.*

## Final recommendation

- **GhostLayer** if you want a privacy-conscious file utility.
- **DiffPaper** if you want difficult document-processing engineering.
- **ProofPack** if you want a developer-focused tool with a clear shareable artifact.

> **Build a tiny tool that completes one job reliably before making a platform.**

### MVP

- [ ] Support JPEG and PNG metadata inspection and cleanup.
- [ ] Show a plain-English report of metadata types detected.
- [ ] Offer selective removal and a preview.
- [ ] Download both cleaned file and optional cleanup report.

### Version 2

- PDF annotations, attachments, properties, and supported document metadata.

**Suggested stack:** Rust + Tauri + React, ExifTool or appropriate file-specific parsers.

**Why useful:** A cleaned file is an immediate, tangible output.

---

## 02 — DiffPaper

**Tagline:** Git-style change review for PDFs.

### Problem

Comparing two lengthy PDFs is hard when text reflows, pages move, or paragraphs are rewritten.

### Single user journey

`Upload original + revised PDF → Match content → Review highlighted changes → Export change report`

### MVP

- [ ] Extract PDF text with page/position information.
- [ ] Match corresponding text spans across documents.
- [ ] Highlight insertions, removals, and replacements.
- [ ] Provide synchronized side-by-side page views.
- [ ] Export an annotated comparison summary with page references.

### Version 2

- Better handling of page reordering.
- Image and table differences.

### Version 2

- Waveform visualization.
- Batch processing.
- Detection and repair of overlapping or invalid caption intervals.

**Suggested stack:** React + Tauri + Rust; FFmpeg optionally for media inspection. 
**Hardest problem:** Correcting timing without creating overlaps, negative timestamps, or unreadably short captions. 
**Why useful:** A frustrating playback problem ends with a tiny corrected file.

---

## 07 — FormForge

**Tagline:** Fill a PDF that was never designed to be filled.

### Problem

Forms are still often distributed as flat PDF documents, leading people to print, fill, scan, and re-upload them.

### Single user journey

`Open PDF → Click empty area → Type/check/sign → Preview → Download completed PDF`

### MVP

- [ ] Render pages with zoom and scroll.
- [ ] Place editable text boxes and checkmarks at exact page coordinates.
- [ ] Add typed date and basic signature drawing.
- [ ] Duplicate/move/resize fields.
- [ ] Flatten entered content into a downloadable PDF.

### Version 2

- Reusable form layouts.
- Alignment guides and keyboard navigation.
- Import/export a local field template.

**Suggested stack:** React + PDF.js + pdf-lib + IndexedDB. 
**Hardest problem:** Accurate positioning when documents rotate, scale, or use unusual page sizes. Distinguish a drawn signature from legally authenticated electronic signing. 
**Why useful:** Eliminates a print–scan workflow in a single session.

---

## How to Select One

Choose based on **how easily you can observe real demand**, not on a novelty score.

1. **Easiest first-use demonstration:** SubShift, FormForge, GhostLayer.
2. **Strongest technical depth:** DiffPaper, ProofPack, NearDrop.
3. **Best fit for a browser extension:** TableLift, ProofPack.

[1] # FreeEdit — Product Improvements & Engineering Roadmap

> **Goal:** Turn FreeEdit into a dependable, frictionless way to clean up a recording and export a shareable result — without becoming a bloated video editor.

**Repository:** https://github.com/srbmaury/FreeEdit 
**Document type:** Product and technical improvement proposal 
**Guiding principle:** **Upload → make a few useful edits → preview → export.**

---

## 1. Product Direction

FreeEdit already targets a clear user problem: quick audio/video cleanup. The existing project, as previously reviewed, includes noise reduction using DeepFilterNet3, video trimming, text overlays, blurring/pixelation, previews, and export via a FastAPI/FFmpeg-based processing pipeline.

**Keep the product focused:** A user with a noisy screen recording should be able to make it watchable and shareable in one session. Avoid accounts, social features, collaboration systems, and general-purpose timeline editing in the first release.

### Primary user journey

1. **Drop** a recorded video or audio file into FreeEdit.
2. **Choose** a quick cleanup action (noise removal, trim, silence cleanup, or privacy masking).
3. **Review** a fast preview and adjust the results if needed.
4. **Export** the finished media with an appropriate size/quality preset.
5. **Leave** with the processed file; account creation should not be required.

**North-star metric:** Percentage of successful uploads that produce an exported file. 
**Secondary metrics:** Median time-to-export; processing failure rate; failed export rate; repeat-use rate (if measured in a privacy-preserving way).

---

## 2. Features to Add (Prioritized)

### P0 — One-click silence removal

**Problem:** Tutorial, lecture, and screen recordings commonly contain awkward pauses.

[2] ependency compliance.

### Phase 2 — Strongest new editing feature

- [ ] Detect silent intervals.
- [ ] Let users preview and toggle proposed cuts.
- [ ] Export synchronized concatenated media.
- [ ] Test edge cases and browser playback.

### Phase 3 — Make sharing easier

- [ ] Build opaque privacy masks with time ranges.
- [ ] Add guided output presets.
- [ ] Show a pre-export summary of changes and expected output.

### Explicitly out of scope

- Multi-track professional editing timeline.
- AI-generated content or AI chat interface.
- Cloud project collaboration.
- Public content feeds or social sharing network.
- Mandatory sign-in for basic edits.

---

## 6. Definition of Success

A first-time user can upload a typical screen recording, remove background noise, shorten pauses, hide one on-screen detail, preview the result, and export a playable file **without help or an account**.

> **FreeEdit should feel like a utility, not a video-production platform.**

## 4. Suggested Architecture

**Keep it simple until there is real load.** A single service can remain the starting point.

```text
Browser (upload + edit instructions + preview)
 │
 ▼
FastAPI API ──> Job admission/validation ──> Bounded processing queue

 ├──> Status and error reporting FFmpeg + noise model

```

**Potential upgrades, not mandatory for MVP:** SQLite/PostgreSQL for durable job metadata, Redis/worker queue for multi-instance deployment, object storage if the platform's filesystem is ephemeral, and WebSockets or server-sent events if polling becomes awkward.

### Data model sketch

```text
MediaJob {
 id, status, input_metadata, edit_instructions,
 output_preset, progress, created_at, expires_at,
 error_code, output_location
}
```

For editing instructions, use versioned typed objects: `Trim`, `NoiseReduction`, `SilenceRemoval`, `Mask`, `TextOverlay`. This makes the frontend and worker agree on what is permitted.

- [ ] Detect silent intervals.

- [ ] Export synchronized concatenated media.
- [ ] Test edge cases and browser playback.

**Problem:** Tutorial, lecture, and screen recordings commonly contain awkward pauses. Manually locating and cutting each gap is tedious.

**MVP requirements**

**Problem:** Screen recordings reveal email addresses, account details, notifications, faces, or other information that users would rather hide.

**Flow:** `Upload → Place mask(s) → Preview full duration → Export`

**MVP requirements**

- Add rectangular **opaque masks**, with optional blur/pixelation for non-sensitive aesthetic use.
- Let masks span selected time ranges, not just one static frame.
- Permit adding and adjusting multiple masks in one recording.
- Offer frame-by-frame or scrubbed verification before export.
- Provide an explicit warning: **blur/pixelation may not reliably protect secrets**. Prefer solid redaction for confidential text and ensure media is re-encoded rather than merely overlaying removable annotations.
- Clarify what is or is not cleaned (e.g., audio speech, metadata, subtitles, other frames).

**Acceptance criteria**

- A masked region is absent from *the rendered output* during the entire chosen time interval.
- Users can inspect the result after rendering.
- Original file is not modified; processing temp files expire safely.

**Technical notes:** Store masking instructions as validated geometric coordinates and time ranges. Translate between preview scale and original pixel dimensions. Include edge-case tests for rotation, aspect ratios, and resolution changes.

## 2. Features to Add (Prioritized)

### P0 — One-click silence removal

**Problem:** Tutorial, lecture, and screen recordings commonly contain awkward pauses. Manually locating and cutting each gap is tedious.

**Flow:** `Upload → Detect pauses → Preview suggested cuts → Adjust → Export`

**MVP requirements**

- Detect candidate silent sections using an FFmpeg `silencedetect`-style pass or comparable audio analysis.
- Display suggestions as segments on a timeline; **do not silently apply destructive cuts**.
- Allow a user-adjustable threshold, minimum silence duration, and padding around spoken sections.
- Support one-click enable/disable of individual proposed cuts.
- Produce seamless combined audio/video output while keeping audio and video synchronized.
- Show the estimated duration saved *before* export.

**Acceptance criteria**

- Original input remains unchanged.
- User can inspect every proposed cut and opt out of it.
- Exported video has no noticeable A/V drift or unexpected gaps in a basic regression suite.
- Very quiet speech is not assumed to be expendable: conservative defaults plus preview are required.

**Technical notes:** Audio analysis → interval merge/filter → edit decision list → FFmpeg filtergraph/concat render. Carefully test nonstandard frame rates, variable-frame-rate video, and silent/no-audio inputs.

## Why jobbot

A typical job search means repeatedly:

1. Finding roles across dozens of company career sites.
2. Deciding which resume fits each role.
3. Filling the same application fields again and again.
4. Answering recurring questions.
5. Remembering which roles you already applied to.
6. Tracking interviews, assessments, rejections, and offers.

jobbot puts those steps into one local workflow.

| Capability | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **300+ companies** | Scans supported job boards and career sites |
| **Resume-aware ranking** | Scores roles against each resume variant and picks the best match |
| **Browser-assisted applications** | Fills supported application forms in an isolated Chrome profile |
| **Validation** | Reads fields back, catches missing/incorrect values, and fixes supported errors |
| **Human-controlled submission** | Stops at the final page so you review before submitting |
| **Application tracker** | Tracks applications, status history, notes, and statistics |
| **Gmail sync** | Imports application-related email into the tracker using read-only access |
| **Local AI** | Uses Ollama for ranking and free-text drafting; keyword matching remains available |
| **Dashboard** | Run scans, review jobs, apply, answer questions, and inspect logs from a browser |
| **AI-assistant skill** | Search conversationally and tailor resumes for individual roles |

5. Remembering which roles you already applied to.
6. Tracking interviews, assessments, rejections, and offers.

jobbot puts those steps into one local workflow.

### Key capabilities

| Capability | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **300+ companies** | Scans supported job boards and career sites |
| **Resume-aware ranking** | Scores roles against each resume variant and picks the best match |
| **Browser-assisted applications** | Fills supported application forms in an isolated Chrome profile |
| **Validation** | Reads fields back, catches missing/incorrect values, and fixes supported errors |
| **Human-controlled submission** | Stops at the final page so you review before submitting |
| **Application tracker** | Tracks applications, status history, notes, and statistics |
| **Gmail sync** | Imports application-related email into the tracker using read-only access |
| **Local AI** | Uses Ollama for ranking and free-text drafting; keyword matching remains available |
| **Dashboard** | Run scans, review jobs, apply, answer questions, and inspect logs from a browser |
| **AI-assistant skill** | Search conversationally and tailor resumes for individual roles |

---

## Quick start

### Requirements

- Python 3.10+
- Google Chrome
- Ollama — optional, for local AI ranking and drafting

The commands below assume macOS with Homebrew.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/srbmaury/target-company-sde-scanner.git
cd target-company-sde-scanner

JORDAN / HISTORY
How the present took shape
EARLIER LIVES AND TURNING POINTS
Petra recalls the Nabataean kingdom and caravan trade. Roman, Islamic and Ottoman
histories followed. The modern emirate developed under British influence after the First
World War. Independence came in 1946. Wars and Palestinian displacement changed the
population and politics; the country later received people fleeing conflicts in Iraq and
Syria.
GOVERNMENT, WORK AND PUBLIC LIFE
The King has substantial authority within a constitutional framework. Services, tourism,
manufacturing, phosphates and external assistance support the economy. Jordan has few
energy resources compared with some neighbours. Employment, debt and pressure on
water and public services remain major issues. Hosting refugee communities brings both
humanitarian responsibilities and practical costs.
Jerash preserves streets and monuments from a Roman city. Its ruins show one part of Jordan’s history before
the modern kingdom.
Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Image record ↗

| P1 | Job state | Persist statuses if jobs must survive restarts | In-memory state can disappear |
| P1 | Validation | Use typed schemas for clip ranges, masks, text, and presets | Prevent malformed or unsafe work requests |
| P1 | Observability | Structured logs, error codes, queue timing, media probe metadata | Faster production debugging |
| P1 | Browser UX | Clear progress stages and recovery from interrupted requests | Users need to trust slow operations |
| P1 | Test coverage | Add media fixtures and end-to-end regression tests | Encoding bugs are easy to miss |
| P1 | Licensing | Audit DeepFilterNet and bundled model/code licenses; add an appropriate project license | Clear distribution and usage rights |

### Recommended job lifecycle

```text
UPLOADED → QUEUED → PROBING → PROCESSING → FINALIZING → READY
 ↘ FAILED / CANCELLED / EXPIRED ↗
```

- Store only necessary state and identifiers.
- Use randomly generated job IDs and authorize access appropriately; unguessable IDs alone are not universal access control.
- Set resource budgets for every job: upload size, decoded duration, memory, CPU time, and disk usage.
- Delete temporary source/derived files safely **after** processing or retention expiry, never during an active job.
- Make duplicate requests and refreshes safe where possible (idempotent submission or job reuse).

---

## 4. Suggested Architecture

**Keep it simple until there is real load.** A single service can remain the starting point.
